content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has conducted and published several epidemiological investigations into the transmission patterns of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV), with additional studies planned or ongoing. WHO emphasizes the importance of sharing the results of these investigations with affected countries and publishing them promptly. Key research priorities include the following: In Dromedary Camels: 1. Conducting natural history studies to assess the potential for reinfection. 2. Investigating the risk of zoonotic transmission from camel products and excretions. 3. Analyzing value chains and production systems to identify critical points for intervention. 4. Enhancing surveillance to evaluate seasonal or temporal variations in viral shedding. 5. Identifying critical points to interrupt within-species and zoonotic transmission. 6. Accelerating the development of vaccine candidates. At the Animal-Human Interface: 1. Mapping the geographic range and circulation of MERS-CoV in humans and dromedary camels. 2. Evaluating the extent of spillover to humans in Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia. 3. Conducting serological and virological studies in specific locations to assess risk factors for human infection and routes of zoonotic transmission, including potential food or oral routes. 4. In Human Populations: 1. 2. Identifying risk factors for infection among healthcare workers in hospital settings and understanding the role of environmental controls in transmission. 3. Investigating the role of asymptomatic cases in human-to-human transmission and whether specific behaviors increase the risk of infection from non-human sources. 4. Conducting targeted epidemiological studies in clinical settings to better understand immune responses and the duration of infectiousness. 5. Integrating MERS-CoV testing into existing respiratory disease surveillance systems in affected countries to identify the extent and spectrum of mild infections in the community. Infection Prevention and Control: Early identification of MERS-CoV cases can be challenging due to mild or non-specific symptoms. Therefore, healthcare facilities should implement clear triage policies for rapid screening and assessment of potential MERS-CoV cases and all patients with acute respiratory symptoms. Standard precautions should be consistently applied to all patients, regardless of diagnosis. Droplet precautions should be added when caring for patients with acute respiratory symptoms, and airborne precautions should be used during aerosol-generating procedures. Contact precautions and eye protection should be used when caring for probable or confirmed cases, and airborne precautions should be applied during aerosol-generating procedures. Cleaning staff should also be trained to take appropriate precautions when cleaning rooms of MERS-CoV patients. High-Risk Populations: Individuals at high risk of severe disease (e.g., those over 60 years old, or with diabetes, renal failure, chronic lung disease, or immunocompromised conditions) should take precautions when visiting farms or markets where dromedary camels are present or engaging in activities involving close contact with camels, particularly in the Middle East and Africa. These precautions include avoiding contact with camels, refraining from consuming raw camel milk or urine, and ensuring camel meat is thoroughly cooked before consumption. Camel Handlers and Workers: Studies indicate that individuals handling or working with dromedary camels are at increased risk of MERS-CoV infection compared to those without camel contact. Camel farm workers, slaughterhouse workers, market workers, veterinarians, and others handling camels should practice good personal hygiene, including frequent handwashing with soap and water or alcohol-based hand gel. Workers should wear facial protection, protective clothing, and boots, which should be removed and washed daily after work. Soiled work clothing and items should remain at the workplace for washing, and workers should use shower facilities before leaving the premises to avoid exposing family members to potential contamination. Camel Infection and Hygiene: Infected dromedary camels may not show signs of illness but can shed MERS-CoV through nasal and eye discharge, feces, milk, urine, and raw organs or meat. Until more is known, the best protection is to practice good hygiene and avoid direct contact with these materials. Sick camels should not be slaughtered for consumption, and dead camels should be safely buried or destroyed. People should avoid contact with camels that have recently tested positive for MERS-CoV until subsequent tests confirm the animal is free of infection. Surveillance and Global Preparedness: Health officials in countries outside the affected regions should maintain high vigilance, particularly in areas with large numbers of travelers or migrant workers returning from the Middle East. Surveillance should be enhanced according to WHO guidelines, alongside infection prevention and control procedures in healthcare facilities. Travel and Trade: WHO does not recommend special screening at points of entry or the application of travel or trade restrictions related to MERS-CoV. WHO guidelines and tools for epidemiological investigations are available on the WHO MERS-CoV website. In summary, WHO emphasizes the importance of a One Health approach, integrating human and animal health sectors to better understand and mitigate the risks of MERS-CoV transmission. Enhanced infection prevention, surveillance, and research efforts remain critical to reducing the spread of the virus and protecting public health.
